utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. And Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-00-39-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Harmon, you're representing the OTP this morning. Are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that that's Mr. Biscevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would have appreciated to receive also the June 2002 statement last Friday and not this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The June 2002 statement, are you referring to the Bosnian statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm referring to the OTP statement with the 13th of December 1995 statement attached to it. The 1995 statement was delivered to the Chamber last Friday, just as another one, but not the June 2002. But I do understand that it's a mistake. But I'm just asking for position in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have something to say before the witness comes into the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've received on Saturday evening a preliminary supplemental information -- well, it was an email containing supplemental information. We've received in a slightly more formal state a supplemental sheet. I make no point about the differences between the two because the later formal sheet only contains a couple of minor additions and adjustments to what was sent to me on Saturday evening. However, what was sent to me on Saturday evening contains a radically different point and involves radically different substance to this witness's evidence as compared with everything that we had previously understood. That is certainly true when one looks at the 65 ter statement, but it goes beyond that because it is true when one looks at the three statements that this witness has given on previous occasions, and in particular, when one looks at his statement which was signed on the 29th of July 1999. The difference, and Your Honours have this material, so there is no -- there need be no disguise about what the difference is, but of course it is extremely important that the witness does not come into Court and create any possibility that he should hear this discussion. In the -- I don't at the moment have a numbered version, in fact, of the statement signed on the 29th of July 1999 except numbered by me, but it's at the foot of the third page of that statement in the English version. The paragraph begins "Vrkes and Savanovic were the SDS leaders who came to these meetings." Does Your Honour see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They said that they never stated that they received orders from superiors."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, and Your Honour sees that paragraph. The first paragraph of the supplemental information sheet which says that Mr. Biscevic met and negotiated many times with the leaders Rasula and others frequently on occasions where a decision needed to be taken Rasula and all the other negotiators would say - more slowly - that they could not decide on their own but they needed to ask others. They would then postpone the meeting and make a decision for one to two days and go to Sarajevo. They would then return with concrete proposals." Now, that point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that that is one of the most important parts of the statement, either in favour or against. Yes, it's clear to me that such surprises are not something the Defence could easily accept at such a late stage. And I think that perhaps part of the explanation would be that since resources are limited in asking the witness to come any earlier, I did understand from a remark of Mr. Harmon last week that the witness only arrived on Saturday. But I fully agree with you, if you would say we would need more time to explore these matters. So let's get started. But if this surprise would disenable you to fully cross-examine the witness or to -- then, of course, additional time should be given either by recall of the witness or in whatever other way. But a remedy should be sought to that. I do agree, from what you tell me now, I haven't received those supplemental information sheet, it's a 180-degree on a very important point. So therefore, feel free to ask the Court to stop or give further opportunity to prepare for further cross-examination when it comes to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, well, I'm obliged, Your Honour. In light of Your Honour's observation, there's no more I need to say right now, or we don't need to debate it. Thank you. At this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So the record is clear, Your Honour, I met Mr. Biscevic on Saturday. Then late morning I discussed the matters with him. I informed counsel as soon as I concluded my discussions with Mr. Biscevic. I gave him an email, and yesterday I sent him a supplemental memorandum. So that is the genesis of the situation. We certainly have no objection if more time is needed to cross-examine this witness. We're prepared to proceed on his direct examination at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps it's also due to the weekend. If a witness arrives two days prior to examination in Court, and usually you find out during the first day of a briefing whether there's something different. But over the weekend, it might be even more difficult to -- but there's no question about if this kind of surprises come up, that the Defence will get a proper remedy to deal with it. Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I do hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Biscevic, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text will be handed out to you now by Madam usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Biscevic. Please be seated. You'll first -- you will first be examined by Mr. Harmon, counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Biscevic.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me begin by asking you about your background, and what I propose to do is summarise biographical information about you and ask you to affirm this is correct. Mr. Biscevic you were born on June 9th, 1940, in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You lived mostly all of your life in the municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are married?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, your immediate family consisted of your wife and three sons?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are a dentist by profession, and at the same time you had a jewellery business in Sanski Most. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I could have you focus your attention first of all on the formation of political parties in Sanski Most prior to the war, I'd like to first of all ask you to describe the ethnic composition of the Municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: In the Municipality of Sanski Most, there were various ethnic groups. The Muslims were in the majority, 45 per cent of the population was Muslim. 42 per cent were Serbs. And the rest were Croats or people who had not decided how to declare themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, prior to the multiparty elections that were held in Bosnia, a number of political parties were formed based on essentially ethnic lines. There was the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ being the major parties. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me at the republican level who the leaders were of the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: At the republican level, there was Krajisnik, Karadzic, Biljana Plavsic, and Nikola Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the Municipality of Sanski Most, did political parties of the HDZ, SDA, and SDS form?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify for the Trial Chamber the leaders of the SDS party in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Nedeljko Rasula was the president, then later on he was the mayor of the municipality. Vlado Vrkes was the secretary, and later he was the president. Vujic -- Drago Vujanic, I think was the name, was the deputy, but there were others. But those were the three persons who at the beginning decided about the SDS party. Drago Vujovic is the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the leaders of the SDA party in the Municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: The SDA leaders in Sanski Most included myself. I was the leader. Hivzo Hodzic was the president before me. I was the first president. He was an acting president. Then there was Suad Sarbic, Mirzet Karabeg. That was the core leadership. Then there was Rasema Cero. That's how it was at the beginning. And later on the party expanded, and other people became member of its organs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long, Mr. Biscevic, did you remain president of the SDA party of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: I served there for one term.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did that term conclude?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you relinquished your position as the president of the SDA, did you remain a member of the SDA main board?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the main board, and I was in the core leadership of the party itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were the leaders of the HDZ party in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: The leaders -- the leader was Ante Tunic. There was Skripa Andjelko and Ivan Filipovic. They on the whole were the president, the vice-president, and the secretary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, following the foundation of the SDS party in Sanski Most, did Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Karadzic come to the municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: When the SDS party was being founded in Sanski Most, in the village Lusci Palanka which is inhabited by Serbs alone, that's where the party was formed. And probably in order to form it as best as possible, the leaders -- the leadership from Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Kosovo came. So they -- there was Mr. Karadzic who spoke while the party was being formed on that occasion, and they contributed to the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have the witness be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 115. This photograph is also being displayed on the monitor, I can see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, can you identify this particular photograph and can you inform the Court where you believe that photograph was taken.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: This photograph was taken when the SDS party was being formed in Lusci Palanka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lusci Palanka is located in which municipality?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: In the Municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify starting from the individual seated at the far left of the image and moving to the right, I'd like you to identify the people in that image, starting at the far left. Are you able to identify that individual?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Nedeljko Rasula, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. -- someone from Croatia. Raskovic. The fifth one, I don't know who he is. The lady there is Krajisnik's wife. The one standing is an official from the municipality in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so the record is perfectly clear, I don't think you understood the way I wanted you to identify these people, Mr. Biscevic. I will identify going from the left side of the image to the right side of the image, the individual. And if you could say I do know this person or I don't know this person, then we'll move to the next person. So starting at the far left, the man seated at the far left, can you identify that individual?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: I can't identify the first one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, moving from left to right, the second individual who is seated at the table and appears to have a beard, can you identify that individual?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a representative from Croatia who came to contribute to the formation of the SDS party in Sanski Most. His name is Mr. Raskovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving to the next individual standing and holding -- appears to be holding a plaque of some kind, who is that individual?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: The gentleman standing is Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving again from left to right, the man standing next to him, who is that?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: This person standing next to him is Mr. Nedeljko Rasula.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was the head of the SDS party you identified in Sanski Most. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was then proposed as president of the SDS party. Up until then, he hadn't held that position. He represented others. It was on that occasion that he was proposed as president of the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the woman seated at the table with her hands -- appears to be almost in a praying position, who was that?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: That's Mr. Karadzic's wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the man next to that woman, again, moving left to right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The woman standing, can you identify the woman who is standing next to Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: That was an official of ours in the Municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I've concluded with Exhibit 115. Mr. Biscevic, in terms of the goals and objectives of the multiparty elections, the Trial Chamber has heard that the communist party was running a slate of candidates. Was there an agreement between the parties of the SDS, the HDZ, and the SDA to defeat the communists, and can you describe what that agreement may have been?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: We know that communism was in power for 50 years in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it was necessary to topple the system somehow. The only way to do so was for the nationalist parties to come together, to form an association of a kind. And this is what happened. For example, no one in Sanski Most knew who Mr. Koljevic or Mrs. Plavsic or Mr. Karadzic were. We knew Karadzic. We didn't know who Krajisnik was. We didn't know Mr. Boris or Mr. Ljubo Ganic. When the lists arrived, then there was a proposal from the party stating whom we should select from the various parties. So these candidates mostly obtained a majority in the municipality and were able to take power. That was the recommendation from above. We implemented it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say there was agreement from above and there was a list, what kind of a list was it that you, members of the SDA, received and what instructions accompanied that list?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: All the parties received it, not only us. There was a complete list of all the parties, and it was said on behalf of the SDS that these people have to go through. They had to be encircled. Others for the HDZ, it said "don't select anyone from the communist list." How we were to proceed was quite clear, and that is how we obtained a majority of votes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were essentially instructed from the SDA party at the national level who to vote for. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that include voting for members of the SDS and the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for all the parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally vote on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you instructed to vote for Mr. Krajisnik among others?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do so?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what were the results of the multiparty elections, and can you describe how those results were implemented in the Municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: The results were very favourable. The League of Communists failed. They didn't get any votes, or almost none. The three nationalist parties obtained votes, and after the votes had been obtained, power in the municipalities were divided depending on the votes that the individual parties had obtained. Since in Sanski Most the population is multiethnic, 40 per cent of Muslims, 42 per cent of Serbs, the SDS Serbian party obtained the majority in Sanski Most. We were aware of this but could do nothing about it, but at the time this had already been rigged because they were probably aware of the fact since they were more literate than we were, they were aware of the fact to obtain more votes. That meant you had absolute power in the municipality and you could do whatever you wanted to do. Since the SDS party obtained the greatest member of votes, Mr. Nedeljko Rasula who was the president of the SDS party then requested that he be appointed as the mayor, and the post of president of the party be given to Vrkes. We agreed to this. The president of the executive committee was Mirsad Karabeg. The deputy of the president of the municipality was Ante Tunic. So that was the first division of power that was made, and these positions were handed out on the basis of the votes. After that, it was necessary to appoint people to the organs of power. The SDS at the time was acting as the number one organ, and they wanted to have the position of the chief of the MUP and of the chief of the military section. These were the next two positions which were the most important ones in the municipality. And they said that they had to be given these positions, and in the end they got them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, following the initial election results, how would you describe the relationships between the SDA, the HDZ, and the SDS party in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, the relationship was correct. There was the euphoria of a victory over the communists. The mayor was the person who was the president of the SDS. Another position was given to the SDA, and another one to the HDZ. However, soon there were conflicts because the SDS always had new requests and always wanting to receive what did not belong to them by rights. So all of a sudden, there were political discords amongst these three parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when there were political discords between the three parties, how would those discords be resolved? What methods would be used to try to resolve those differences?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: I was the president of the SDA, Suad Sabic was the president of the representative group. And Mirzet Karabeg was president of the executive board. In the SDA, we made decisions in a regular way which were not disputed. However, there were always problems with the SDS. So whenever there was a conflict and when we couldn't agree on a certain position, then they would say we cannot agree to things before we consult our party members. At the beginning, we didn't have a problem with that because we thought that this was a legitimate procedure, and we would ask them "who is it that you have to consult?" However, we never learned who they had to consult. But the fact is that they would come to the following meeting with a decision that they got from somebody that a certain kind of compromise could be reached on a position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during the period of time of these negotiations and differences of positions between the SDS on one side and the SDA and the HDZ, I take it you were negotiating with Mr. Rasula who was the head of the SDS party for Sanski Most and others in positions of power in the SDS party. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. His advantage lie in the fact that he was a mayor besides being the president of the SDS. His decisions were obeyed and were implemented the way he wanted them to be implemented. He was the one in charge of the politics in the municipality, not only of the politics in the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at times when there were disagreements on significant issues where compromises had to be made with the SDA party, are you aware of whether Mr. Rasula left Sanski Most and went to some other location?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rasula was the mayor. He did not have to explain his acts. He didn't want to tell anybody -- he didn't have to tell anybody where he went. Nevertheless, he did go somewhere every week. He didn't tell us where he went. It did happen. It was a common practice that he did go away on business. He had his chauffeur. He had his car. He could go wherever and whenever he wanted to go. He did not have to explain himself to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of his going to Sarajevo or to Banja Luka or to points outside of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He would mostly go to Sarajevo and to Banja Luka because this is where the higher levels of government were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did -- now Mr. Rasula never stated that he had received orders from his superiors. But did you and other members of the SDA attempt to find out whom Mr. Rasula was consulting, and what was Mr. Rasula's response to those attempts?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: We never doubted for a second that he went to the higher levels to consult. Whenever he said "I can't take a decision without consulting somebody at a higher level," we always supposed that it will be somebody from his party. However, later on it turned out that it wasn't, that it was somebody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to find out with whom he was consulting?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at some point in time, you have described the relations between the various political parties, the SDA, the HDZ, and the SDS as starting out harmoniously and then the relationships changed. And you said that the SDS party was making more and more demands. During that period of time, can you recall a conversation that you had with Mr. Rasula's secretary in which he made comments directly to you?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: The situation got more acute. On one occasion, amongst the items of the agenda, there was an item according to which Sanski Most should become part of the west Krajina region. It's centre was in Banja Luka. We reacted quite strongly. We said we did not want to belong to that region because most of the municipality already belonged to the Banja Luka region, and we knew that the centre of all the Serbian ideas was in Banja Luka. We were supposed to reach a party -- an interparty consensus. We as a party went to a different room to try and reach an agreement. When we started discussing the matter, our proposal was for Bihac to be the centre, and the SDS proposed Banja Luka as the centre. Mr. Rasula's secretary Mr. Drago Vukic who has a degree in economics, and he worked as a secretary, he was a member of the main board of the party, he was also a representative in the municipal assembly, he told me on that occasion, "Faik, we don't want to live with balijas in Alija's state. We are all going to die. Not you." I was dumbfounded. I knew that he was intellectual, so I didn't understand what he meant. I had asked him "what is it that could happen to you in this state?" He didn't say anything. He just said "we are all going to die if we continue to live in the -- in Alija's balija state."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The term "balija," is that a pejorative term for Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a derogatory word for Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you to focus your attention on the war in Croatia that was taking place. The Court has heard a lot of evidence about those events. But in Sanski Most, what effect did the war in Croatia have on the stability in the Municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Sanski Most is in Western Bosnia, very close to the Croatian border, and this is only normal that the developments in Croatia had an effect on Sanski Most. There was this war in Croatia, and we knew it. We felt it. And as the SDS volunteers started volunteering as members in the JNA in order to fight a war, they would stay 10 or 15 days on the front line. When they returned, they would be drunk. They would have beards, long hair. A lot of them had cockades on their heads. They all carried Kalashnikovs, automatic weapons, and when they arrived in lorries, there would be celebratory shooting. There would be a lot of drinking. There would ill treatment of people, provocations, and we did not find that pleasant, to say the least. And then the population of the Sanski Most Municipality were asked to join the JNA. When we saw what was going on and what was being done, we said to the Muslims and to the HDZ that we would not respond to those call-ups to wage the war in Croatia. If we were to be mobilised in the Municipality of Sanski Most, then we would do that. If not, we would not go anywhere under such conditions. What happened next was the JNA when we realised that they couldn't mobilise people, they said "very well, then. Those who didn't want to be mobilised, they should return their uniforms, their weapons, and they would be deleted from the mobilisation lists." We agreed to that. And it was an occasion for the Serbian able-bodied men to be mobilised to the ranks of the JNA. The procedure was as follows: As they returned from the front lines, they became more and more bold and daring. So in addition to their drinking and celebratory shooting and provocations, in Sanski Most during the night, Muslim and Croat business premises were being destroyed and blown up. There were some 20 or so that were blown up at the time, and the perpetrator was never discovered. The chief of the MUP was a Serb, a member of the SDS. The chief of the military department was also a Serb, a member of the SDS. We asked from them to organise joint patrols during the night. We wanted to see who was it that was doing those things. They told us "don't interfere with our work. We know what we are doing. As soon as we discover the perpetrator of these things, we will let you know who they are." At the same time when Muslims and Croats refused mobilisation, an order came from the command in Belgrade or in Banja Luka for all the weapons of the Territorial Defence that was to be found in companies and in local communes to be surrendered to the military department and stored there instead of being with the citizens. Even the guards who were standing guard in various companies were also disarmed. In simple terms, the population was disarmed in every possible way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I take it from your testimony that there was little, if anything, done to control the unruly soldiers coming back from the Croatian front, those soldiers that you described as "destablising" the situation in your municipality. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely fair. When they arrived, they had full power because they had JNA uniforms on. They had all sorts of bands, white, black, and red. The civilian population did not dare say anything to them because they had the right to shoot and kill them. And they were the ones who introduced this destability in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in early April, did a unit of the JNA arrive in the Municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: We were informed from Sarajevo that a large convoy of the JNA was moving through Bosnia. Interestingly enough, this convoy started from Jasenovac during the night with their lights off, and they were moving through the less-densely inhabited areas with less Muslim population. However, we knew that they were moving, and we were following them from Bosanska Dubica. We were monitoring their movement. They set off in the evening, and they arrived in the territory of Sanski Most in the local commune of Lusci Palanka. After that, after a day or two maybe, Mr. Rasula invited me and the other leaders of the SDA to join him. And he told us that representatives of the JNA were coming. This meeting was held during the day. Mr. Basara came from there. Major Zeljaja came from Prijedor. Captain Dragan came from Banja Luka. They said that they had arrived in the territory of Sanski Most. According to them, they wanted to give their troops a rest after having spent some time in the front line. They wanted to repair their weapons and clean them, and he also said that they had nothing whatsoever to do with the developments in Sanski Most. According to him, they were simply following orders. We listened to them --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Mr. Biscevic: You said they arrived in the village of Lusci Palanka. Is that a Serb village?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 100 per cent Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they make their base or their headquarters in that village?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: We didn't know that. We only knew that they were deploying their troops and weapons on the hilltops around Sanski Most in the villages with the Serbian population. This is where all the weapons were deployed. Interestingly enough, later on when we held our meetings, they were always attended by Mr. Basara. He attended as the representative of the government. If there was a conflict or some sort of discord at those meetings, he would tell us "we guarantee peace in this area. We will not interfere with politics. However, we will prevent any conflicts because we are here to protect the interests of all the ethnic groups in the territory of Sanski Most." This is what he used to tell us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... I'm sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, may I ask you the following, Mr. Biscevic: The last question was about whether the headquarters were in that village. The beginning of your answer, you focussed on that question. But then you went on exactly to say whether or not Mr. Basara was attending what kind of meetings and what position he took, et cetera. That was not the question. We are under some time constraint. Could you please carefully listen to the question. If you have answered the question about the headquarters, if Mr. Harmon would like to know about what Mr. Basara did or did not, he will certainly ask you. So could you please focus on the question, answer that, and then wait for the next question to be put to you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, the Court has heard a lot of evidence about the arrival of the JNA and the people who made up the JNA in Sanski Most, but just so the record is perfectly clear, you've mentioned Basara. What position did he have as far as you knew in the JNA unit that had arrived in Sanski Most? What was his position?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there subordinate officers to Mr. Biscevic -- I'm sorry, to Mr. Basara who were from the Municipality of Sanski Most? And if there were, could you identify who they were.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukic. He was captain from Tuzla. We met him when there was an attack on Sanski Most. But there were reservists, citizens of Sanski Most who had already had ranks. And as soon as they were mobilised, they kept those ranks and under those ranks they joined the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your previous answer before Judge Orie intervened, you said -- you testified that the army representatives, Mr. Basara included, had said that the army was here to protect the interests of all ethnic groups. Was that the public position that the JNA took?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a different agenda in your opinion? And if so, what was that agenda of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: The time would show that the agenda was totally different. It was as clear as a bell that the agenda was to occupy, militarily occupy the area of Western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to focus in the next series of questions I have for you, Mr. Biscevic, and have you describe the role of the JNA and the SDS party in the arming of the Serbian citizens of Sanski Most. Can you describe the respective roles as you understood them, and can you incorporate in your answer any observations, personal observations you had, about the arming of the Serbian citizens of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: They stopped hiding it. Helicopters would arrive every day either in the territory of a Serbian local commune or the -- a playground in Sanski Most by the MUP. They refashioned a bus. They put tin plates instead of glasses, and they used this bus to distribute weapons amongst the Serbs in the Serbian villages. And that happened every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You personally saw the bus and you personally saw the landing of the helicopters in Serb villages?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: I saw helicopters. However, nobody dared approach them. I saw Mico Krunic who was a retired policeman who was in charge of that. And I saw that bus moving around every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what was in that bus?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you describe to the Court a meeting that took place in the village of Kruhar. First of all, identify what ethnicity was the majority population in that village, and can you describe a meeting that took place in that village in respect to the provision of arms.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: The village of Kruhar is a Serb village. A meeting was held there. However, there were also three Croat houses there. When the meeting was called, a Croat citizen went to that meeting. He didn't know what it would be all about. Mr. Rasula came, and he said to the citizens of this local commune "I'm capable of arming you within two hours and with those weapons you would be able to wage a war for five years." This Croat citizen was dumbfounded. He didn't know what would happen at that meeting. However, as soon as the meeting was over, he came to us and he told us what Mr. Rasula said to these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me read you a quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour and counsel, this is a quotation from an exhibit. It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 65, tab 221. This is a quotation of General Milan Gvero at the 34th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. This was held on the 29th of September 1993. And in his speech to the Bosnian Serb Assembly, General Gvero said the following: "The Serbian democratic party and the established state institutions also have the most credit for the initial arming of the Serbian people with small arms which was possible thanks to the support and cooperativeness of numerous Serbs. Officers in JNA commands in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbs in the interior ministry, and other political institutions and offices of the army of Serbia, that is to say, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." I won't read more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is General Gvero's quotation consistent, Mr. Biscevic, with what you saw and observed and understood to be the case of arming in the Municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's all consistent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during the period of time when the Bosnian Serbs were being armed by the JNA in coordination with the SDS party, did Muslims and Croats request arms from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: No, no they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they provided other arms by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me focus your attention then on another topic, and that is the takeover of the MUP, the police, and the Territorial Defence. Can you inform the Court what happened in respect of the takeovers of those particular institutions. Can you describe that to the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rasula, Mr. Nedeljko Rasula came in front of the MUP with the troops armed with Kalashnikovs and said "from now on, this is the Serbian MUP. The MUP of the Serbian state of western Krajina. All the Croats and Muslims who are willing to sign and pledge loyalty should sign or leave." Only one Croat pledged loyalty. The others didn't, and they had to leave. They were chased out of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the result of the takeover of the police station? What effect did that have on the municipality?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: There were political meetings later again, and we said that if they were taking the MUP building, the building of the Territorial Defence on the grounds of the MUP, that's a military section, we wanted the SDS or the HDZ to take that building then, and they didn't allow this. Since there wasn't an agreement about this issue, we then decided to take the building of the municipal assembly which was located in the centre of the town. And we took over this building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "we took over this building," who is "we"?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: The SDA, the HDZ, and MUP employees who hadn't signed the pledge of loyalty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any violence or force used to take over the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was political negotiating for two days. There was an SDS delegation. We tried to reach an agreement on how to divide things up and we couldn't reach an agreement. On the second in the evening, there was a gathering before the building, a gathering of troops, armed troops, Next to the municipal building there is the post office building which very high and a hotel. That is where we noticed sniper nests, machine-gun nests, and there were troops. The square was full of troops. They had encircled the municipality. We were in the municipality. They were on all other sides. At 10.00, Rasula phoned and said "leave the municipality in 10 minutes' time or you will be destroyed and burnt in the municipality." At the same time, a Zolja was launched into the basement area. When this was done, the members who were in the assembly withdrew, and they went to the Muslim village of Trnova Sesto.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were in the municipal assembly building at the time it was attacked by the -- you said Zolja, which is a rocket. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were about 30 or 40 people there. It's difficult to say exactly how many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were personally present, were you?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: No. I was travelling. I was on a trip so I wasn't there that evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the information you've related to the Court is based on information you received from people who were present in the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the following day, we talked about this because they returned. On the following day, nothing happened. It was calm. But at the square in Sanski Most, we could see the flag of the Serbian state of Western Bosnia, and the same flag was flying from the MUP building. It's interesting to point that out. So as they said, by flying these flags, they had given legality to their takeover of power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Court has heard the considerable evidence about the date of the takeover. Can you recall the date of the takeover of the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: I think it was on the 19th of April. I think that is when the municipality was attacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the significance? You mentioned there were flags, Serbian type of flags flown over various locations in the municipality. But what was the real significance of the takeover of the municipal building? Did that change the power structure in the municipality of Sanski Most as far as you were concerned and the HDZ was concerned?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: From that time onwards, the SDS had complete power. We didn't have any power. We weren't allowed to go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there announcements made in respect of which laws now applied in the Municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: On the following day at daybreak, they told us that Mr. Talic was coming from Banja Luka and that he wanted to have a meeting with us. He really did come, and he said that he was guaranteeing security for all the citizens of Sanski Most. He said that this was a JNA guarantee. But since the SDS had taken over power without authorisation of any kind, without having consulted with anyone, they took over the Sanski Most radio station whose director was a Muslim. They took the SDK service whose director was a Croat. These were the first steps that they took in order to take over power. So they had funds available, and there was propaganda, and they broadcast announcements over Sanski Most radio from that day onwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From that day onwards, Mr. Biscevic, were the HDZ parties and the SDA parties partners in a democratic system of ruling the Municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: The SDA and HDZ didn't have power of any kind any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me -- you mentioned removal of people from -- non-Serbs from positions of power. I'll come to that in a minute. I'd like to focus first of all your attention on the efforts to disarm the non-Serb population, populations of Sanski Most following the takeover of the municipal building in April of 1992. First of all, can you describe to the Trial Chamber, was there a campaign to disarm the non-Serb populations of Sanski Most, and can you describe what it was, how it took effect?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the campaign took place every day. There were announcements of Radio Sana. For example, the Otok settlement on Monday at 5.00 in the afternoon at such and such a checkpoint. For example, all citizens were supposed to take legally and illegally owned weapons. My settlement is the settlement of Otok. I handed over my hunting weapons. We didn't have anything else. Then a civilian vehicle with a trailer arrived. Things would be put on to the trailer. A man in a military uniform appeared. He didn't issue a certificate of any kind for any of the weapons that were handed over. This was current practice in all the villages and all the streets where there were Muslim and Croat inhabitants. Patrols went around gathering illegally and legally owned weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say it happened in all the villages, did it happen in Serb villages, this campaign to disarm the citizens of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were the locations -- how were the areas that were identified for disarmament identified? Was that -- you mentioned a radio broadcast. Were there other means in which citizens were informed when they had to submit their hunting rifles and their legal and illegal arms?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the fact that they announced where there would be checkpoints in various areas, every day there was an announcement stating that weapons could be taken to the MUP premises and to the premises of the military section. They said that there wouldn't be any questions, that people could quite simply hand over these weapons which were illegally or legally owned and that they wouldn't suffer consequences of any kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you turned over your weapons. Did your sons turn over any weapons they might have had?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: My eldest son and myself, we were hunters. We had weapons which we had permits for, and we handed these weapons over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any receipts for those weapons?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you describe for the Court very briefly the events in the disarming of Trnova. First of all, is Trnova -- what type of village is Trnava?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: It's inhabited by Muslims alone. It's a large village. And someone told them that there were two guns in Trnova. It's interesting to point out that they always said "bring your weapons." And "bring" meant that the weapon was either a pistol or a rifle. Yet they claimed that the Muslims and Croats were armed. They never said "bring your weapons." On one occasion, they heard from that village that they had two guns, and they asked them to bring those guns. It's a Muslim custom when praying to fire from a gun so that the entire population would know that it was time to starting eating. So these were made of cherry wood. They were 60 centimetres long. You would put a little paper and gunpowder in the gun and set it alight and the gun would then fire. Those were the only guns. There was a man who worked on this, and a man who was half mad and didn't know how to do anything else. When they heard of these guns, he took this gun, he put it on his back and took it to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we comment here. Ms. Cmeric confirms that whatever the merits or demerits of the answer, it made perfect sense in the witness's own language as delivered. It doesn't really make a great deal of sense in the English translation on the transcript, certain aspects of it. Just to put down a marker there that that particular answer will need some particular attention when the transcript is reviewed because it really doesn't work in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I notice that in the supplemental information sheet provided to us, it's about a cannon, where here the translation says it's a gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you -- yesterday when you and I, or Saturday when you and I spoke, you described the gun as a cannon. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: It was a cannon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the information that the Serbs were aware of was that there were two cannons in the village of Trnova, not two guns but two cannons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: They claimed that there were two cannons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then an announcement was made. And can you tell us -- strike that. Then you described a man who was, I think in your words a minute ago, half mad. Did he take that cannon made of cherry wood and turn it into the Bosnian Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: He took it to the police. He handed it over to the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I think that's a more accurate description of the event as opposed to what was translated. Now, let me continue with this line of inquiry, Mr. Biscevic. In response to weapons being turned in, what assurances were given by the local governmental authorities and the JNA to the people who had turned in their weapons? What types of guarantees were given?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: They provided verbal guarantees for the security of the citizens of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of the announcements on the radio and the request to various Muslim and Croat portions of Sanski Most to turn in their weapons, by the time the attacks in Sanski Most started in May, late May of 1992, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond were most of the villages that were non-Serb disarmed?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in terms of -- again focussing your attention on the post -- the period following the takeover of the municipality building and leading up to the period when active combat started, you mentioned that there had been the removal of at least two non-Serbs from positions. You mentioned, one, the radio station, and two, you mentioned a Croat woman from the SDK. Were there other non-Serbs removed from positions of authority in government and in private business?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: All Muslims and Croats, all positions in the Municipality of Sanski Most were removed. They were replaced. At the gate of the medical centre one morning, there was a soldier, and all Muslims and Croats, all the doctors could no longer enter the building. In the school, it was the same. In the public utilities building, it was the same. In the fire brigade, it was the same. Wherever the Muslims and Croats, access was prohibited. They were quite simply drawn away from their jobs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was removing these people from their jobs? Who was responsible for the removal of those people from their positions?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: On the whole, either Vrkes or Rasula would appear with the troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me focus now your attention to an attack on the Mahala that took place on the 26th of May 1992. First of all, was the Mahala a Muslim quarter, Muslim section of the village of -- the town of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Trial Chamber an announcement that was made over the radio in respect of what the people in the Mahala had to do to show their support to the Serbian governmental authorities in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: The announcement was that weapons should be handed over at checkpoints. Whenever they gathered those weapons, they would say "there are extremists who haven't handed over their weapons. Hand your weapons over or the troops will come to take them away by force." This was a pretext for them to do what they subsequently did. On the 25th in the evening, there was an all out attack on Sanski Most. They fired from all kinds of weapons from all sides, from all directions. My family and I were in the garage. That's where we spent the night. My friend, Mehmed Alagic was with me, Dr. Mehmed Alagic. He was later killed. And my children and wife. At 7.00 in the morning, the attack stopped and there was an announcement made over the radio according to which Gornji Mahala hadn't handed over their weapons. There was an ultimatum according to which the weapons had to be handed over by 11.00 otherwise Gornji Mahala would be attacked in order to take the weapons from the extremists by force. The scenario was quite different since Otok and Mujici and Gornji Mahala were linked. The Muslim inhabitants lived there. The troops went from house to house, and they said that -- they asked for all of the inhabitants to come out, men, women, and children. Whoever didn't was killed. If someone hid somewhere, and if they subsequently found that person, he would be killed. When they had driven the population out, there was a training ground near Sanski Most which is fenced in. That's a training ground for drivers. And all the population from that area was taken there. That population was transported later on to Krings, some to the hall, some to the central prison. They were moved out immediately by buses. A column of five buses had already left at that time. On that day, the attack against Mahala took place from 11.00, as I said, and lasted until 3.00 or 4.00. On that day, 192 houses were destroyed and set on fire and looted. 192 houses were set on fire and destroyed, so the entire Gornji Mahala was destroyed. In Kuzelj, there was one inhabitant from that part who had hid in a manhole. They found him and they eliminated him. In Mujici, there was someone else. They let him go, but when he came out of the barn they killed him. Farko Malicevic didn't go to the training ground. He went across the field of the training ground, they killed him, too. Whoever remained, they killed him, whoever didn't go to the training ground was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they killed him," who do you mean "they"?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: The Muslims, the inhabitants of those villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they killed them," who killed the Muslim inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs in military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was there an announcement in respect of sheets, bed sheets?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When the attack on Gornji Mahala was supposed to take place, there was an announcement before that that stated that all the Muslims who were loyal to the Serbian State should have white signs, white flags in front of their houses. So many of those Muslims and Croats took white sheets and had them flying from their houses so that one could see that they were loyal to prevent shooting from breaking out and to avoid being killed. But this was a signal for them so that they could know which house was Muslim and Croat house and which one was a Serbian house. They didn't want to destroy any Serbian houses. Later when they were shelling the houses, they knew exactly which houses had to be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, are we going to go until 10.30? Is that what the schedule is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, 10.30 is the usual time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, I'm going to ask you about 7 or 8 minutes of questioning, and then we're going to take a break. We're going to interrupt part of your testimony. But let me just ask you, on the 27th of May 1992, were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe your arrest, please.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: I said that that evening I was in the garage with my family. I was there with Dr. Alagic. At 7.00, the shooting stopped. Things calmed down. We went to the kitchen to have something to eat. But at 11.00, they announced that there would be an attack on Gornji Mahala since the weapons hadn't been handed over. They said this would take place if the weapons weren't handed over. When the shooting started at 11.00, we went to the garage again because there was shooting from all sides. And there was a danger of being hit. Since my house wasn't secure, we were in the garage. After 12.00, there was an attack. But before that, my son "father, see the troops passing by. But there is no attack going on here." I didn't pay any attention to this. After 12.00, we went to the garage again, and we heard that someone had broken down the entry to our house. My wife went to see what was happening. When she went out, they said "Faik needs to report immediately. They need him at a meeting." I went out. I put a coat on. When I went out, I saw that the troops had arrived from all directions. And I think that there were four vehicles there. There was a white Mercedes in front of the gate. They put me in the middle. On each side there were two uniformed troops. There was one in front and there was the driver. When I sat between them, when I sat down between them, they said that they had been ordered to put handcuffs on me, which they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: First they took me to the MUP. They put me in the hall in the MUP, told me to face the wall. There were many troops who were swearing, beating people. After a while, they came back. Took me and put me in the car again. They took me to the Magarice village. That was the name of the village. That's an elevated, hilly area on the periphery of Sanski Most. When I reached that village, after they had taken me out, when I got out, I first saw that there were many troops there because the troops passed by there. Later on, I found out that their command was located there. When I got there, I saw that there was a big table, and there was a litre of cognac and a map of Sanski Most on the table. Mr. Basara and another officer were sitting there. Later I found out that this officer was Captain Major Lukic. When I said good day, he cursed my balija mother and he shouted at the troops. Why have you handcuffed him in front? Do it at the back and make it tight, as tight as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, the only question put to you is where you were taken. You're now describing the behaviour of other persons. I'm not saying it's not important for you, but we are under some time constraints. So please, listen to the question. And please, Mr. Harmon, keep a bit better control.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would have asked that question next, but he anticipated the question. So at least Mr. Biscevic saved us -- me the time of asking that question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Mr. Biscevic always knows exactly what questions you're going to put to him but I can't imagine that you would not have asked him again whether someone was cursing, whether -- perhaps some details might have been a bit repetitious. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continue, if you would, just describing the events upon your arrival. You indicated that an officer complained that you had been handcuffed in the front. What happened then? And can you describe the events that followed.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: He then stood up and took me next to that camp to an opening. I saw there were a lot of troops there. There were military crates that had been lined up. 1 metre by 2 metres. And then there were the small cannons used for firing rockets at the town. I saw that they fired on the town from that area. I saw that it wasn't necessary for them to be in Sanski Most. He told me "see what you have done to Sanski Most. See what this has led to." There was nothing I could do. When he returned me to other soldiers, they took charge of me and they took me to an orchard. These were soldiers who were supposed to beat people. Since they had brought in two other people, the scenario was the same. I could see that this was current practice among them. And naturally they took me away and they beat me so badly that I broke the handcuffs. When they returned me, then the captain appeared. He asked me to stand by a table. He gave me a piece of paper and side write down the following. I didn't know what I was supposed to write.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. This is a good time to break. I want to just fill in a couple more details and then we'll get to that part of the story in just a minute. When you say you were beaten, how long were you beaten? What period of time?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: It's hard to say for how long. At least half an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many troops were in the area where you had been brought? How many did you see?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Wherever you looked, there were troops everywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct to say that from the location where you were -- had been brought, you could look down into the village of -- into the town of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: That was an elevation, and there isn't a forest down below, so you could Sanski Most, the entire town, very clearly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated that at that time, the troops from that location appeared to be shelling into Sanski Most. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any shelling coming out of Sanski Most back to the firing positions where the Serb soldiers were firing?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: No, they were singing, drinking, laughing, having fun. Because there was no danger of a bullet hitting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, this would be an appropriate time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. We'll adjourn until 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, before we proceed with your continuing to recount the events of the 27th of May, I would like to go back in time and ask you again a question or two about the period relating to the multiparty elections. And following the multiparty elections or before the multiparty elections, did you ever have occasion to meet the defendant in this case, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: On one occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe to the Trial Chamber the circumstances of that meeting, who introduced you, when it was, where it was?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Soon after the elections, I was the president of the party. Mr. Rasula was the president of his party. And when we travelled to Sarajevo together, we came across Mr. Krajisnik and I was introduced to him. This was our only contact. It was not a conversation. It was just an introduction. But I knew that that was Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person who introduced you to Mr. Krajisnik was Mr. Rasula?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let us return now to the 27th of May 1992. And I want to take you back to the point where you said that after you had been beaten, you were returned and asked to stand by a table. A captain gave you a piece of paper and asked you to write. So can you tell us what happened to you from that point on.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know what I was supposed to write. He came to me. He took the piece of paper. He took a gunfire burst by my ear, and said "this awaits you and your family if you didn't read this." I didn't know what "this" was supposed to mean. First I was beaten. And I don't know. I didn't know what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after he gave you the piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Again, the two soldiers took me, put me in the car and took me to the radio station of Sanski Most, which is downtown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that point in time, who controlled the radio station?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: The SDS did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened at the radio station?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: At the radio station, I was placed at a desk. I was given a piece of paper with the text that I was supposed to read into the microphone. And this is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, if we could pass out the Prosecutor's next exhibit. It is an audiotape. And it has a transcript associated with it. There are two parts of the audiotape that we're going to play. And I can direct Your Honours' attention -- I don't know if Your Honours have copies of the transcripts already. If that can be distributed, then I can direct Your Honours to the portions that we will be playing. And likewise, if Mr. Biscevic could be given a copy of the transcript in B/C/S. Your Honours, let me direct Your Honours to -- we're going to play two portions of this tape. The first portion we will be playing starts on page 5. There should be a shaded area on page 5 that runs over to page 7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Biscevic, for your information, the first portion of the tape we're going to play appears on page 9 of the B/C/S version and runs over to page 11. Then we'll pause. Then we will play a second portion of the tape. That portion in the English version has been highlighted. It starts at page 9 and goes to page 10 in the English version. And in the B/C/S version, Mr. Biscevic, if you turn to page 15 and 16 of the B/C/S version, that will be the second part that will be played. If we could play, then, the first part of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Your Honours will see that we're going to start above, two segments above the portion where Mr. Biscevic starts. It will start with a female voice, then there will be a male voice. Then there will be Mr. Biscevic's voice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And a male voice will conclude the first segment. If we could play that first portion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, if you could follow along in the transcript, and then I'm going to ask you some questions to identify about this tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, can I take it that the interpreters' booths have received copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "If not at exactly 18.10 hours we will begin to show the village. If the order is not complied with we will not bare a moral or material responsibility for the consequence of the shelling. Male Voice: "The Serbian armed forces have captured the greatest Muslim and Croatian extremist in the Sanski Most Municipality. Faik Biscevic who attempted to flee from the town. This extremist will address the Croatian and Muslim peoples over the radio and explain the reasons why he involved them in the war. "Announcement. That all Muslims and Croats unconditionally hand over all the weapons they possess legally and illegally and that they surrender to the Serbian Army and government because this is a Serbian town. To avoid the soldiers having to use force to locate and seize weapons, it would be better to hand over the weapons voluntarily, otherwise Sana will continue to be destroyed until final capitulation. That is why we call upon all the citizens of Sana, Muslims and Croats, to hand over their weapons straight away which would be better for them than to have the town continue to be destroyed. That is why I ask you to see reason and without delay hand over all the weapons and surrender to the legitimate Serbian authorities. This has to be done immediately. The weapons have to be handed over in order for the destruction of the town for which I bear most of the blame, to cease. "That is why again I call on all Muslims and Croats to immediately hand over their weapons and recognise the legitimate Serbian authorities so that the legitimate authorities can start functioning as soon as possible and the destruction of the town can end. The Serbian armed forces guarantee the safety of all loyal Muslim and Croatian citizens, and I recommend to Alija's and Tudjman's extremists, and I am their greatest follower in Sanski Most, not to lead their people into further bloodshed. "I, Redzo Kurbegovic, Mirzet Karabeg, Suad Sabic, Hasib Kamber, Ferid Burnic, Enver Burnic, Nihad Kljucanin, Ekrem Medic, Nedzad Muhic, Eniz Sabanovic, Ahmed Paunovic, Hase Osmancevic, Fahrudin Prsic, Arif Hodzic, Hidajet Dudic, Arif Muhanovic, Fikret Agic, Muhamed Smajlovic, Muhamed Arapovic, Mehmed Alagic, Ibro Pasic, Omer Krupic, Enisa Kurbegovic, Ibro Krickovic, Vahid Fajdo Badnjevic, Safet Avdic, Vahid Handanagic, Suad Cehic, Ismet Ico Avdic and his two brothers, Tale Zahirovic, Muharem Handanagic, Taib Crnkic, Hamza Rekic, Fuad Kurbegovic, Osman Talic, Dervis Hamzic, Elhad Talic and Basic, I don't know his first name, but he worked in the Borac Travnik in Lusci Palanka are guilty for everything that has happened recently. That is why we are prepared on the orders of the Serb armed forces to come out before our people and to be judged by our people in the next few days. "I assure you that the command of the Serbian armed forces which is carrying out the armed activities in Sanski Most was forced into such behaviour by our lies and sycophancy. I call on all my sympathisers to join me, to surrender to the command of the Serbian armed forces since that is the way we can stop the further bloodshed of our people. "Sehovci, Poljak, Sasina, Pobrijezje, and Caplje, are to collect all the legally and illegally obtained weapons..."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In respect of this particular transmission, there's a part of the transcript that is attributed to you. You've heard the audio transmission. Was that your voice?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the statement that you were forced to read on the 27th of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you draft that statement or did somebody draft that statement and give it to you?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: It was waiting for me at that desk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any information on who drafted that statement?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to play now a second portion of the tape. And if you turn, Mr. Biscevic, to page 15 and 16, you can follow it. It should be shaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Your Honours, it is the transcript portion of the tape that is highlighted on pages 9 and 10. And if we could start that, I'm going to ask you some questions about that. If we could play that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "...their legal and illegal weapons to the Serbian authorities. Not to fall prey to Muslim or Croat extremists, nor to the tale they tell because that would lead to the suffering of innocent people. We have now shown who and what we are, accusing and blaming one another. Our people have seen through us and don't trust us any longer. That is why I ask you to respond to the legitimate Serbian army and authorities. The Serbian army has already made a few announcements and has given us the opportunity to surrender, so please, heed the appeal and hand over your weapons to the command of the Serbian army where I have been staying for two days now and I'm personally convinced that it is the most humane army I have ever met. "The exclusive blame for all the sadness and pain inflicted on the Muslim and Croat peoples lies with us who did not have the instinct or the brains to extend the hand of reconciliation to the Serbian people who generously held out theirs to us. The words I'm saying are my own. And the officers and soldiers of the Serbian armed forces with whom I have spent the past two days have helped me see the truth. Announcement written by Faik Biscevic."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In respect of the second portion that was just played, Mr. Biscevic, were those your words?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the circumstances under which this statement was prepared.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: On the second day, I was taken out of the room where I was. They placed me at another desk, and the captain gave me this written text. Because the second time, I didn't go to the radio station. I read that out at the Magarice. I didn't know that this would be aired on the Radio Sana. And later on, it was indeed broadcast, and it was broadcast in the way to show that I had been at the radio station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you to -- first of all, let me ask you, were the sentiments that were described in both of these statements your sentiments or were those sentiments that were essentially -- you were forced to express in these transmissions?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: At the time I did not have an occasion to see this. But one can tell that it had been drafted by an expert who had a goal in mind. I didn't have anything to do with the drafting of these two texts. I just read them out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you read the first text, you had been taken down to the radio station. You read the text. What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Again, I was put in a car, but this time it was not the troops that took me in the car but a policeman whom I knew personally. He put me in a Golf car, and he took me towards Magarice. One part of the road is asphalt; the other is not covered in asphalt. He -- we stopped at the asphalt part, and he told me that I would be taken over by the army. However, when I got out of the car, the troops saw me. They shouted "Oh, here is a balija we have captured." And they wanted to slaughter my throat. One of them was very aggressive. He cursed my balija mother. He told me that his sister and his brother-in-law had died in Ilidja, a village near Sarajevo, and this is -- was a good opportunity for him to take his revenge.
