When the policeman saw what this was all about, I suppose that he -- his orders were that he should bring me to Magarice alive. So he returned me to the car, and then he drove me to the top of Magarice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That's -- Magarice is the village where the Bosnian Serb Army, where Colonel Basara was located. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is where the command was and the kitchen was also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have the exhibit number, by the way, of the tape and the transcripts just for recordkeeping purposes before I continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The tape is Prosecution Exhibit Number P274. The transcript, P274A in the original B/C/S, and P274.A.1 for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you returned to Magarice, describe your treatment and conditions, please.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: When the two soldiers brought me there, the car had remained some 15 metres away. They marched me to the prison. I had broken my handcuffs. They were surprised to see that. So they tied my hands with a rope. So they carried me more than allowed me to walk. When we arrived, the captain wasn't there, only Basara was there. And he said "don't do that. Take this man down to the prison." They said "no. He has to stay here according to the orders of Captain Vukic." They put me in a room where a dry kiln was. It is where meat is dry-cured. It is a wooden room with pebble stones on the floor. They threw me down there, and this is where I was kept for two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Describe the conditions. Were you given food? Were you given water in those two days? Be very brief.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: No. There was no toilet. I was not given any food or water. I was not even allowed to lie down. I had to sit. I could not stand up, so I was half awake all the time. Only on the second day, around 12.00 in the night, the two men that were brought to that same place later on and I were taken out. And they put the three of us in three separate cars. I was sitting in the middle. On my two sides were two armed soldiers with Kalashnikovs, and the third soldier was sitting in the back. And they all had their guns pointed at me. They were probably afraid that I would try to flee. And they took me to the central prison in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in the central prison in Sanski Most? Until what date?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: I stayed there until the 27th of August, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the conditions in the central prison in Sanski Most where you were detained.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived at the central prison in Sanski Most, it was past midnight. I found in my cell all the leaders who had been placed there before me. The room was 4 metres by 2 metres. It had an iron door. And there was an opening where a window used to be. This was covered in tin sheet. And there were just holes pierced with a 4-millimetre drill. This was our only source of air. There was no electricity most of the time. There was no water. At first, we would be taken three times a day to be given food and to relieve ourselves. And later on, they didn't do even that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you the next two exhibits, please, in order. They are photographs. And I would ask you to identify those photographs for us, please. If we could start with this photograph, and if I could have a number on this particular photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Photograph bearing ERN number 01249099, Prosecution Exhibit Number P275.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if I could have the other exhibit also shown to the witness, which I assume will be P276, we will proceed with the examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, Witness, Mr. Biscevic, starting with the first exhibit which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 275, could you identify this exhibit and inform the Trial Chamber what this represents.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: This is the corridor of the central prison. You can see two cells, and the third one is behind the glass with an iron door. At the far end, you can see the entrance to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we take a look at the next exhibit, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 276, can you identify that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Here you can see the iron door. There was no air. And you can see this tin sheet through which we received air. That was the biggest problem. We did not have enough air to breathe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was that tin sheet with the perforations in it the only source of ventilation in the cell where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: The only one, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men were detained in the cell with you? And the cell I'm talking about is the room depicted in Prosecutor's Exhibit 276.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Every day there were interrogations, so they would bring new people every day. The number, therefore, differed. There were up to 20 people at times. We didn't have any air. We kept standing all the time. And we would usually move in a circle all the time so that each of us would come close to those tiny perforations through which the air was coming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were brought into that Sanski Most prison on or about the 29th, I take it, the 29th of May, and you remained until the 27th of August. Were there ever any formal charges brought against you or brought against any other person who was in that cell as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, when we were there, we were interrogated. But there were never any official charges brought against any of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in the Sanski Most prison and went into that cell, can you identify some of the other people who were present.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: At that time when I arrived, there was Jakupovic, there was Suad Sabic, Redzo Kurbegovic, there was also an engineer called Ceric. There was a Croat who used to work at a bank. He was among the first ones to be brought there. Unfortunately I can't remember his family name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who were detained in that cell, were they soldiers? Were they civilians? Can you characterise their status for us, please.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: They were mostly party leaders. But there were also people who had nothing to do with the party. For example, Ico Jakupovic was one of those. The Croat that I mentioned had nothing whatsoever to do with any of the parties. They were mostly intellectuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, coming back to my question, Mr. Biscevic, were they soldiers? Was there status as armed combatants? Were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you give us a general description of the sanitary conditions that were made available to you and to the other prisoners who were in that particular cell throughout the period of your detention. I'm talking not only sanitary conditions, I'm talking about food, I'm talking about what shower facilities were available to you, what toilets were available to you. If you could summarise, please, for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived, there was nothing in the cells. The last room that you see is the toilet. It was very messy. There was a lot of paper thrown around. And the toilet was used, and the ante room was full of excrement and paper. In order to be use that, we had to clean this room with our hands. There were a lot of us there, and the cells were full. And this one toilet could not be used as it was supposed to be used. So behind our cell, they forced us to dig a 2-metre deep hole which was 2 metres long and about 1.60 centimetres wide. They placed two wooden boards there, and this is where we relieved ourselves. During the 60 days, I was given just one opportunity wash myself, and that was towards the end of my stay. So what I'm saying is that for the 60 days I stayed there, I did not have a change of clothes. I did not wash myself properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the same as to the other detainees who were in that particular cell?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: There were three cells there, and this applied to all of them, the situation was the same for all the people in all the three cells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of your detention in the Sanski Most prison, did you lose weight?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: I lost 32 kilos during that 92-day period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man by the name of Emir Seferovic?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Most of the leaders were captured and brought in very early on. Hasan Kamber who was the secretary of the party and Emir Seferovic who was a religious leader were brought to the third cell some 20 days later. When they were brought in, Seferovic suffered the most because he was the religious leader. He was always taken out more than the rest of us to be given food. That food was the leftovers from the officers' food. And most of the times, the food was pork. So this poor guy was given that food, that pork to eat. They would force him to eat pork, and they laughed at him and ridiculed him and they would say "look at the Hodza," how he eats pork.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was a Hodza from a particular village or from Sanski Most? Where was he from?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: He was from Vrhpolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you and Mr. Seferovic and others were detained, were detainees beaten?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was an everyday practice. Everybody could beat us. We enjoyed a special treatment. And according to the rules, the shift leader was the only one who had the key. However, after the working hours, they would bring the troops in and the troops beat us. And this especially applied to Kamber and Seferovic because they were brought in after us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was responsible for the beating? Can you identify the organisational unit from which these people who were beating you were associated?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: We didn't know who they were. Whoever wanted to get to us did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they civilians or soldiers who were -- or police? Are you able to give us any enlightenment as to the organisational units that these people were associated with?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: They were in military uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you have occasion at some point in time during your stay in the Sanski Most prison to examine the condition of Mr. Emir Seferovic, the hodza?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: As I said, we received special treatment. In 15 minutes, all three cells had to go out, have breakfast, relieve ourselves, and then go back to the cells immediately. The cells would be locked -- or the cell would be locked and another would be opened. Then the International Red Cross arrived, a representative came, and they allowed all of us to go out into the yard. One by one they took us into the cell with this representative, and we were able to talk there. On that occasion, I saw Emir. He said that his jaw hurt, that it had been broken and that he couldn't open and close his mouth. As I am a dentist, I was able to approach him then and have a look. I saw that the mandible arch had been broken, that the bone was broken. And this was the reason for his pain. But there was nothing I could do. All I could do was take note of the fact that the mandible had been broken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thereafter, did you see Mr. Seferovic again?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Not alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn to the next exhibit, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit -- it should be 277.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This exhibit, Mr. Biscevic, is a record of the identification of a body. It was made on the 2nd of June 1998 in Sanski Most. Can you identify this particular exhibit and tell the Judges the circumstances under which this exhibit was created.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: This is in English. Is there a translation into B/C/S? Yes. This is an original record that I drafted. It came to light that in the village of Trnova, there was a cemetery. It was opened up, and two bodies were found there. Asim Kamber, the brother of Hasan Kamber asked me to go identify the body since I was with him. And I said that the Efendi had had a broken jaw. He wanted to see whether I could tell whether it was his brother whether it was Efendi. When I went there, when I examined the body, I saw that to the left the jaw had been broken. And I said that it was Efendi Hodza. When we had a look at the second body, since they had been registered by the Red Cross, too, we could then find a certificate from the Red Cross with the Efendi. And then we saw that it was Asim's secretary, that was the first body, and his jaw was also broken on the left. Whereas in the case of Emir, when I examined him, on both sides there was a fracture of the mandible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is the official record of the identification of Mr. Emir Seferovic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: An official record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we could -- let me continue to explore with you a little bit your stay in the Sanski Most prison. Did you have occasion to see any Bosnian Serb political leaders come into the Sanski Most prison?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: As I said, we were in a corner, whereas the yard was large. And there was a kitchen there where the policemen and officers and the troops would go to eat. Initially, we saw Nedeljko Rasula, who would go there to have a little food. We didn't have any contact with him because he was over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in a position to see the detainees?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Of course he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your earlier testimony about the prison, you said when you arrived, many intellectuals were being detained in the Sanski Most prison. Can you tell me in terms of intellectuals what you mean by that term first of all.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: People with a university education.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were the people who were detained in the Sanski Most prison people who were leaders in the non-Serb community?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: There were leaders of the party of democratic action, and intellectuals who had absolutely nothing to do with the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber the fate of the non-Serb intellectual community of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Many of them were killed. And they were all driven away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why they were killed?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they probably wanted an ethnically clean area in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, after you left -- I'm sorry. Can you tell the Trial Chamber when you left the Sanski Most prison and where you went.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: On the 27th of August at about 10.00, a duty officer arrived, and he said that we should all get packed, that we were leaving. When we sent out, we saw that they were coming out from the other cells and a bus had been brought into the yard and the door was open. They said we should go in one by one and sit down in the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think there were about 12 of us at that time, 12 of us who were receiving this special treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go once you got on the bus?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: When we got on to the bus, we first went to the Krings prison. That was a hall in an industrial zone, and there were far more detainees there. And they detained them together with us. And then they took us to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, earlier in your testimony, you said you had three sons. Briefly identify them and what their professions, occupations were at the time in May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: My eldest son Haris was a graduated dentist. He had his own business in Sanski Most. Edin and Nedim, the other two sons were twins. And they studied at the university of stomatology. They were fourth year students.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had they been arrested in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: There was this gathering in Sanski Most, they were all gathered and taken to the hall. And I was taken to the prison.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The two sons studied at the university of dentistry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges the fates of your three sons?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: The eldest son Haris and one of the twins, Nedim, were taken away on the 6th of June. That was with the first convoy that went to Manjaca. It was the first organised convoy. They were taken there in lorries, and they were taken to Manjaca. The twin Nedim stayed in Manjaca. When they got there, there were beatings everywhere, and then they called out six or seven persons, I think. Six or seven of our citizens. My son Haris Biscevic was called out. They put them in the lorry again and took them away from Manjaca. And to this day, we don't know where they were taken to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you seen your son Haris since that period of time?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: I haven't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to your other son?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: The other son remained in Sanski Most. And on the 7th of July, when there was the final gathering, a large convoy set off consisting of six lorries also in the direction of Manjaca. He was in one of the lorries, one of the lorries collecting detainees from the Betonirka premise. It had a tarpaulin, which was hermetically sealed. The other lorries were open. And as they had been collected at 10.00 in the morning, it was only at 5.00 in the afternoon that they arrived in Manjaca. And they were kept under that tarpaulin for the entire day without water, without air. And people suffocated. Masses of people suffocated under the tarpaulin. My son wasn't in that lorry. He was in another one. When they arrived at Manjaca and when they saw that the people had suffocated, the leadership of the camp panicked, but there were four of them who were still showing signs of life. They then cried out, "Is there a doctor here who can help?" As my son was a doctor, he responded, and used artificial respiration to bring them back to life. They then put those four people and my son back in a lorry and took them away in an unknown direction. Those who had suffocated, we found the cemetery where they had been buried, whereas the four persons giving signs of life and my son didn't return to Sanski Most. They haven't returned to Sanski Most to this day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of that son?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Nedim Biscevic. Edin Biscevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to have the next exhibit in order, please. And this --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number P278 and P278.1 for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This exhibit deals with your third son Nedim Biscevic. Can you identify this exhibit and explain the circumstances of its creation.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Occasionally officers would come from Banja Luka. They would come to the camp and call out certain detainees asking them to come out. And one day, they appeared and they called out my son's name. I wasn't there at the time. And they put him in a car. Vojo Kupresanin took charge of him, the president of the Assembly of Krajina. They took him to Banja Luka to my sister's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you acquire a copy of this document from your son?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's an official copy stating that he's being released from Manjaca. There is the signature of the officials who authorised this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And therefore, of your three sons, this was the only two son who survived the events of the war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe briefly to the Trial Chamber the fate of your wife during those days.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: As I said, they were all collected in Sanski Most. My wife was taken to the Krings hall. And from the Krings hall they gathered the women and men over 60 years of age. They put them into the buses and took them to Bosanska Krupa. She ended up in Velika Kladusa where I think she spent about five months. She was then taken to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you remained in Manjaca until what date?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Until the end of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to your being released from Manjaca, were you presented with some sort of a form to sign?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't, but everyone had to sign a form saying that we wouldn't be returning to Bosnia because they said if you ever return you'll be killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who gave you that form?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: An official from the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, have you since returned to the Municipality of Sanski Most, and do you reside there today?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after its liberation, I returned there. And that is where I live now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to show you the next exhibit. It's a previous exhibit. It's Prosecutor's Exhibit 209.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I meanwhile ask some clarification from the witness. You said you remained in Manjaca until the end of August. If I did understand you well, you arrived on the 27th of August. Would that mean that you stayed for only a couple of days in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, until November. Until the end of November. It was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That has now been clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Just to be sure, Mr. Harmon, from what I remember from last Friday, P209, the seal has been lifted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know if Defence counsel has a copy of this at hand. If not, perhaps the English version could be displayed on the ELMO so they can see it, and we can -- I can question the witness on the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would turn to -- put on the ELMO, first of all, so counsel can see it, the front page of the document. And -- yes, it's there. And then if you could turn, Mr. Usher, to page 2 of that document and display page 2 of the document on the ELMO. Let me ask you to inspect this document, Mr. Biscevic. This is a document that has previously been exhibited before the Trial Chamber. It was prepared in May of 1993 by the Republika Srpska Minister of the Interior. It is a list of citizens who have moved out and into the area covered by the sector. And if you turn to page 2 of that document under IV, under Sanski Most, you will see that it says "moved out, Muslims, 24.000; Croats, 3.000; Serbs, data n/a; moved in, Serbs, 5.000." Does that appear to be an accurate estimation of the numbers of non-Serbs who were forced out of the Municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: I think it's very accurate, very precise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me turn, then to another area, and that is the area of religious facilities that were existing in the Municipality of Sanski Most prior to the conflict starting in May of 1992. Approximately how many mosques and Catholic churches were there in the Sanski Most Municipality?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: In the Municipality of Sanski Most, there were 26 mosques, 4 Catholic churches. They were all completely destroyed. Not a single Serbian religious institution was destroyed up until then or after the liberation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were taken after your arrest and you were taken up to the elevated area where you encountered Colonel Basara and you could Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond see down into the village, were you able to see a mosque that had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Captain Vukic asked me "do you see the mosque in Trnovo?" Because you can see it from everywhere. He said "you'll never see it." I said "I can't see it." And he said "you'll never see it again. It's been destroyed."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had that mosque been intact prior to the shelling of the Mahala and the attack on Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me focus now finally on one other area, and that is I'd like you to affirm for me certain losses. I'd like to focus if I can on the impact of these crimes on you, on members of your family. And let me just focus briefly on the material losses that you suffered because you, as I understand it, you can correct me, you were a wealthy man in the village of Sanski Most prior to the conflict erupting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read a list, and all I'd like you to do is affirm for me what I have to say. Your material losses included the following: Your house and your dental offices and your dental equipment were either destroyed or burned. You had a jewellery store. That was looted and burned. You had 200.000 deutschemarks worth of gold as part of the assets of your jewellery store that was stolen. You had a cottage on the river that was looted. You had a farm with two houses and two stables. That was looted -- those buildings were looted and destroyed. You had significant livestock, approximately 130 sheep, 60 goats, 600 chickens, three cows, two calves, five dogs. Those were stolen or killed. You had farm equipment, a truck, a tractor, a cultivator, and other farm machinery that was stolen. You had a bus. That was stolen. You had the following motor vehicles: A Mercedes car, a Fiat car, two Jeeps. That was stolen. Your material losses are estimated to be in the range of 1 million deutschemarks. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: At least that much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have described the tragic loss of your two sons during these events. I'd like you to describe if you can, if you want, the impact of the loss of your sons on you and the surviving members of your family.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we're living as we have to do after experiencing the camp, the terror. We're not dead but it's as if we have been killed. It couldn't be worse. The children are not present. That's even worse. I don't know where they were. If only we could bury them like normal people. All we do is listen about the -- to information about the location of mass graves, wonder whether they will be found. I was a healthy man. After having left the camp, I now live with the help of medicine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you comment on the effects of these tragic losses on your wife.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: My wife has been bearing this stoically. As she weighs 45 kilos, she lives as she has to live.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, can you describe to the Trial Chamber the effects of these crimes on the social fabric of the community of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: In Sanski Most, the community was a mixed one. We lived in harmony. I had many Serbian and Croatian friends. My family was mixed. My sister's daughter was married to a Serb, et cetera. I thought this was quite normal. These ties are now broken. Contact is gradually being established, contact of a sort. People are returning to their homes. No one bothers them. They live quite freely in Sanski Most. Those who committed crimes, and that's the majority, they quite simply can't return. So their houses have been abandoned. It's ugly to see them. The inhabitants who have returned live miserably, they don't have a pension, they don't have houses, they don't have money to fix them. They live in ruined houses, and also with nylon covering them. So they're just surviving. The effect on the whole community has been very negative. This will be put right, but it will take some time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you focus just briefly on the effect on the Serb community in Sanski Most, the effect of those crimes as you see it presently.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC
utterances.text: If the Serbian leaders who were in that area and the ones in the federation could return to their Serbs to Sanski Most I would like that. And then we would see what they would experience and how they would fare because those who aren't guilty are now suffering. They can't put up with their leaders now. I'd like it to be possible if they could go and be among them so that they could see what they did to their own people, to the Serbian people. Last Sunday -- last week, as I'm a hunter, there was a man who died in a Serbian village. One man buried him. He was standing there all day. There was a dead man lying there all day. No one was there to bury him. And that is the responsibility of those leaders. That's what they did to their people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no additional questions, Your Honour. I've concluded my direct examination. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Biscevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, would you like to have a short break, or can we continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can continue. That's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stewart, are you ready to start the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, Mr. Biscevic, we suggest, should leave the Court at this point anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it there's an issue you would like to raise at this moment. Mr. Biscevic, there is a procedural issue the Defence would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would follow the usher for the time needed, and we will call you back as soon as we're ready with that issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's, of course, precisely the issue that was raised immediately before this witness gave his evidence this morning. Now, I recognise, on our side anyway, that there are now, if you like, at least three versions. There is his original statements. There's what we were notified over the weekend. And there's what he actually said in evidence this morning. And they're all a bit different. On the other hand, what he said this morning, although falling slightly short of, if you like, his proof of what we were notified over the weekend, is still essentially the radical departure from the way in which his evidence stood before he came here. Your Honour, the question is not, and I have absolutely no reason, cause, to criticise Mr. Harmon for the work done over the weekend and the fact that these matters came up over the weekend. When Mr. Harmon said this morning, and I'm paraphrasing, that he had done what he could over the weekend to notify us, and so on, I don't quarrel with that at all. But that's not the point. The point is -- we do comment of course that although no doubt financial constraints all over the place have an effect on when witnesses can be brought here as well, they shouldn't have a devastating effect on the ability to pick up the telephone and talk to the witness in another country. But the -- but that's -- the essential point is where we are now, and where we are now is a very different witness. And Your Honour, the chief -- the possibility of compartmentalising cross-examination, that's not -- with respect, that's not the -- a possible cause or an appropriate course because -- but the fact that inquiries need to be made and the fact that this witness has, in effect, gone into a different category means that the -- the overall approach to his cross-examination may need to be revisited. So even though in theory one could take small, encapsulated bits of his evidence and deal with it in cross-examination, that's not, with respect, a fair approach. The Defence must have the opportunity of investigating these matters, and then we must have the opportunity of assessing our approach to cross-examination before this witness is cross-examined. And, Your Honour, so far as timing is concerned, that typically -- such inquiries, and of course we do make inquiries, we're in communication with people in Republika Srpska and elsewhere. We find that typically they take one or two days. That's the norm. And of course, we have to do some translation work in each direction as well. That's done fairly speedily because, of course, we do have people on hand to do it. But we do find that typically is takes one or two days to obtain material, sometimes it's a bit quicker, sometimes, of course, it can be significantly slower if people need to travel. But Your Honour, it does put us in a position where it simply isn't feasible for us to proceed with cross-examination of this witness during this session. When I say "this session," this session which is now breaking until the 20th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, two things. One, I do believe that cross-examination can proceed. There are a number of areas that are discrete. There are areas dealing with, for example, the elections, the arrangements that had been made up to the multiparty elections. There is the takeover of the municipal building, the takeover of the MUP, the war in Croatia and its effects, the arrival of the army in Sanski Most which has been the subject of considerable testimony prior to this. I can remember detailed testimony of Witness 628 in that regard. There is discrete areas of the arming of the Serb population in Sanski Most, again, a subject of considerable testimony by Witness 628. There is an area of the disarming campaign. Again, the subject of considerable testimony by Witness 628. The area of discrimination against the non-Serbs, once again I direct your attention to the prior testimony. The circumstances of Mr. Biscevic's arrest, the statement that he was compelled to give over the radio, his conditions in the Sanski Most prison have all been outlined in his statement that the Defence has had for a considerable period of time. The conditions in the Manjaca camp and the circumstances of Manjaca, also detailed there. So there are considerable areas where cross-examination can and should continue in our view. On the issue of what is the material difference that is cited by counsel in the statement that was -- of Mr. Biscevic's, and Mr. Stewart kindly directed the Court to bottom of page 3, and the statement reads, in the second sentence of the bottom paragraph: "The SDS leaders never stated they received orders from their superiors." That has not changed in terms of the testimony. "No political leaders from Banja Luka or other high-ranking visitors came to these meetings with the SDS." That has not changed. "I concluded that local leader -- SDS leaders went to Banja Luka for meetings but I cannot give any facts about that." He didn't give any facts about the meetings that took place outside of Sanski Most. So there may be a difference in the nuance, but in terms of the substance of his testimony today, it is not significantly different that it requires an adjournment for the whole cross-examination of this witness. So our position is clear -- it is that the cross-examination should proceed today. If there is a particular element that the Defence feels so disadvantaged by the information revealed in the testimony or the supplemental information sheet, we don't have an objection to a brief delay. However, I understood that the hearing is scheduled for today; it is not scheduled for tomorrow. I understand that members of the Trial Chamber, and I will not be available either for the remainder of this week. My view is that the cross-examination should proceed today, and we should conclude as much of that as possible. If there is an area that needs additional investigation, then we can consider how much time, if any, should be granted for an adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say, first of all, a textual analysis of what's said in that paragraph and what has subsequently been said is not the point. I referred specifically to that paragraph because as matters stood before this witness gave evidence, there was a clear difference. But even without that paragraph at the bottom of the statement, the point is that this is an entirely new piece of his evidence. It's an entirely new approach. Textual analysis is really not the point. It's quite clear, as Your Honour recognised earlier this morning, it's quite clear that there is a 180-degree turn, it's quite clear that this witness has been moved into a very different category in relation to this absolutely critical element of the case which involves links. It's also as I submitted, Your Honours, a few minutes ago, it's quite inappropriate to compartmentalise cross-examination. Many of those areas -- in fact, as matters stood at the moment, as listed by Mr. Harmon, I probably wouldn't cross-examine about at all. But without wishing to go into some sort of account of a way we might approach this witness, but Your Honour knows that every witness in cross-examination, in effect you make a decision whether you're going to say that the witness is lying, whether he's mistaken, whether he's confused, what mixture of that. And when a witness changes his category and the thrust of his evidence changes the opportunity is required, apart from obtaining necessary information, to reconsider that aspect of the matter as well. And it may be that matters which didn't require cross-examination on the evidence as we were expecting it to arrive up to the weekend do then require cross-examination. It could be that the converse applies, that the whole question of a witness's cross-examination then has to be reconsidered. So far as timing is concerned, well, it may be unfortunate that here we are without the opportunity, although -- well, I say it's unfortunate. In fact, it's we -- if we had been able to continue later on in the week, that would still raise the question of whether the witness should stay here in The Hague for a few days or should go home and come back and so on, so there may not be much difference. But anyway, the fact is apparently we can't. The -- it isn't just a question of hour or so to obtain information. We can obtain, of course, Mr. Krajisnik's immediate instructions, and we've made arrangements to do that. Of course we can do that. But that's not -- that's not the point. The point is we will, and I'm absolutely -- I'm sure about this, Your Honour, we will need to make inquiries of our people, if I can put them that way, our people out in Republika Srpska. That's -- it's certain that we will need to do that. And it is certain that that cannot be done in the matter of just a few hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think the Chamber will have to withdraw to take a decision. But from what I understand -- of course, when I gave this morning -- when I made an observation about the 180-degrees, then, of course, we did not know yet the testimony of the witness to come. What I do understand that at this moment -- and in his statements, the witness said that the SDS leaders never stated that they received orders from their superiors, whereas in the supplemental information sheet he says that when he was talking about SDS leaders, they that they frequently on issues where a decision needed to be taken, Rasula and all the other negotiators would say that they could not decide on their own but they needed to ask others, whereas in his testimony of today he said about such consultation that he supposed that it would be someone from his party. However, later on, it turned out that it wasn't, that it was somebody else, although when asked he said that he had not found out who. But I do understand it was not someone from the party. I think these are the three changing positions in the course of statements, supplemental information --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I make one observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't wish to interrupt Your Honour. May I make one other observation, that I would after all be entitled to cross-examine this witness on something. I'll consider of course to cross-examine this witness on discrepancies that -- among the three points, really, what's been given in statements before, what's given as to -- in the supplemental information sheet, because after all the witness can hardly deny that that's what he said to Mr. Harmon over the weekend, and what he said today. Now, Your Honour, I can't fairly be expected to enter into cross-examination of this witness, for example on any discrepancies between what he said over the weekend and what he said this morning, without my having an opportunity to find out what our position is and what my instructions are. I can't be expected to take the risk of exploring those matters without the opportunity of knowing what our position is and what information I will get in response to those inquiries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for a short while, and then the Chamber will decide whether or not the Defence is required to start cross-examining the witness. --- Break taken at 12.14 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber grants the request of Mr. Stewart to postpone cross-examination as a whole. I add to that immediately that the fact that new information appears in a supplemental information sheet, even if that would need further inquiries, would not under all circumstances bring the Chamber to a decision that cross-examination could not be started. It is, therefore, the general remarks on -- I always have difficulties in pronouncing that word - compartmentalising, it's a difficult language for me as well - that splitting up in specific compartments, that's easier to pronounce when the -- that would not be acceptable in the -- in general terms, that is not a view the Chamber adopts. So for future events, if a similar thing would happen again, then this decision could not be understood as accepting that general principle. On the other hand, it is also clear that here we -- the Defence has had no opportunity to verify with those persons with whom the witness may have been negotiating and may have been speaking at that time, that there was no reason whatsoever to verify with the other participants in such negotiations or meetings whether they would have ever said anything apart from -- so therefore that that certainly takes some time. The Chamber is aware of that. And of course, it might be such an important issue that the approach of the witness, the approach of the cross-examination might be affected by that. It is the expectation of the Chamber that if we would start here, that the issue is of such importance that there's hardly any chance that after verification the witness would not be recalled, even if those inquiries would not result in a lot of things, then of course it would have -- it would lead to quite a lot of questions on how at this moment he says this is why and another moment he says a different story. And of course, you are to reserve those questions until after verification. The Chamber is aware of that. So since there's hardly any chance that the witness would not be recalled, at least that's our expectation at this moment, it's also for the practical reason that the Chamber, where it would be quite hesitant to send the witness back and have him recalled unless that would be really necessary. But understood the present circumstances, and also in view of the practical consequences, the Chamber grants the request. I'd like to briefly explain to the witness what happened, and I'd also like to instruct him. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Two things, Your Honour: One, I wasn't aware the Chamber would be granting that. But in anticipation that it could, and possibly would, I've looked at the schedule when it would be convenient, given the other witnesses who are scheduled. The dates that are available on our schedule would be the 30th of September and the 1st of October would be the two first dates that would be available. Second of all, I would appreciate it if the Chamber could inform the witness that the Prosecutor -- parties are not to have consultations with him and cannot talk to him until the conclusion of his cross-examination so he will understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say the 30th of September, 1st of October. And what would be the next day? The 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Those would be the two dates, Your Honour. I anticipate that the cross-examination would not take more than two days. So those are the two dates that are available for us in terms of scheduling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Examination-in-chief took approximately two and a half hours. It was indicated to start with for four hours. And then it was reduced on our last sheet to three hours. But I can imagine that the issue at stake would make it a bit more difficult to apply the 60 per cent, if not rule, then at least the 60 per cent practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Guidelines, Your Honour. We always have this -- this verbal difference. The -- what your -- I would say, so far as it might be helpful, Your Honour, that although the point is important, it wouldn't necessarily take a long, long time. So I would be quite hopeful that the 60 per cent guideline would be broadly met anyway. Certainly, two days seems most unlikely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I will consider that. If you start with the witness in the morning, if we would have a morning session, that he might even be able to return home on that same day. Also, because the Chamber is not led by financial issues, as may come clear from this decision already, at the same time the Chamber shares a responsibility with the parties not to waste unnecessarily any time or money.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, since I'm on my feet, may I just mention very, very, very briefly, so far as the dates are concerned for scheduling this witness, we -- we have no -- no observation at all. That -- those dates, if we're notified via counsel, that creates any problem. We note what Your Honour says about compartmentalisation which is a word which itself probably requires to be compartmentalised. The third point, Your Honour, is just that I -- I take it that of course we understand entirely the -- the fair courtesy to the witness in explaining how it is he's being sent away, but I take it that Your Honour will only be giving him the very barest indication of why it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll not set out to him in detail, although it's part of the public session by now. But it's -- I'll just instruct him in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: One last item, Your Honour, before the witness comes in, if Mr. Stewart could inform us before the -- well before the arrival of the witness, approximately how long he anticipates taking, then we can schedule perhaps other witnesses behind that, if it's going to be one hour cross-examination, we will find ourselves without a witness for those remaining portions of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So that's a courtesy I would request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course, no problem at all about that, Your Honour. We shall do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I do not know exactly, but I take it the witness would be sent back again since it would be almost 14 days, that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I suspect he would like that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Victims and Witnesses Unit, unfortunately, thinking that it was already a lunch break took the witness to the place where he resides. If the parties would agree that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber wants to explain to the witness what happened and to instruct the witness. Of course, we could now wait until it's 2.00 and have a whole new team of interpreters and technicians at our disposal and to send them away again after five minutes, the Chamber prefers the parties to remain stand by to see whether we can get the witness into the courtroom witness the next 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a couple of very short points that I would like to raise with the Trial Chamber anyway, so if this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we could use that time. If Madam Registrar -- I excused Madam Registrar because she will try to do whatever is needed to get the witness back. And then we could use our time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll make sure to speak slowly for the courtesy of the interpreters, so -- courtesy as well of Your Honour, that will -- perhaps the witness will be here. The first point, Your Honour, was simply to clarify something in relation to -- and I'll be careful what I say on this, Your Honour. There is a motion for protective measures in relation to a particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And we had raised the question the other day about -- and there was a certain amount of discussion related to ex parte and confidential judgements. And we understood Mr. Tieger to be saying that a decision which was made about four or five months ago was not material, didn't fall to be considered for the purpose of this motion. I said at the time that if it wasn't absolutely, 100 per cent clear that nobody was going to be relying on anything in that decision or any of the material leading up to that decision, except, of course, as far as it is specifically reproduced again for the purpose of this motion, then we didn't have a problem with this. But we are slightly concerned about whether that could really -- not questioning anybody's integrity or anything like that but whether that can really be the intention because the motion itself expressly refers to that decision, recites that the Trial Chamber had found that the witness might face retaliation and harm if the identity was disclosed, and so on, and then footnotes what happened. And we are slightly concerned about this, Your Honour, and it may be that the more satisfactory position is to go back to what we were asking for originally which is what -- which is that we should get to see this material, because under the present timetable, and it is our intention to meet it, we have to respond to this tomorrow. And we're ready to do that subject to completing our work in relation to this particular matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll try to see whether we can -- first of all, the Chamber will look at the matter with -- I would say, with Defence counsel eyes, if you would -- I still remember from the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if your response is due for tomorrow, of course, if we have some difficulties, we'll look at it this afternoon and see whether we can give you any different message apart from go ahead as you initially wanted to go ahead, that you have to see that decision before you can respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes indeed. And, Your Honour, it's important -- we are, as I say, equipped to do that, and our work is very far advanced, subject to this, and we need to do that anyway because the witness is due when we come back. The second point, or maybe it's the third point, but again, it's very brief, Your Honour, in relation to another witness whose number is, was, 625, we have in the past asked on a number of occasions if there was going to be a report back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, it was a matter which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree with you, that we should still spend time on it. If there would be five or ten minutes left before the witness arrives, we might turn into closed session to deal with it. I do understand that we have still 10 minutes. Is there any other issue you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That was my shopping list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am reluctant to comment on a motion that was argued with Mr. Tieger. He's not here. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are now dealing with another issue. Let's first turn into private session. I think private session will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I be excused for just a minute. I may be able to intercept Mr. Tieger who's on his way down, and I can at least brief him about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We are in open session. The witness has not yet arrived. In order to prevent us -- perhaps we could just have a short break. And the Chamber will be standing by, if the parties could also be standing by, and as soon as the witness arrives, we'll return. --- Break taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, I apologise that as a result of a misunderstanding that you thought that you would have your lunch break, and that it now turns out that matters are different. When we asked you to leave the courtroom for a while, in your absence, the Defence indicated that they would need a bit more time to prepare for your cross-examination, and the Chamber has considered that and has granted a postponement of cross-examination. I'm not going to explain to you exactly for what, but that's the situation. And under normal circumstances, this would have meant that you would have to wait perhaps for one day or two days, and then the cross-examination could be finalised. But it's a very unfortunate coincidence that the Chamber will not sit any more on from tomorrow until the end of next week. That means that your cross-examination cannot be postponed just for one or two days, but it has to be postponed for a longer period of time. So I take it, although I'm not responsible for matters in relation to leaving and coming back, but most likely, I think, the Victims and Witnesses Unit would ask you to come back at a later stage. That could be in approximately two weeks. First of all, I'd like to ask you whether you would be available to come back in the time as I set out. That would mean from now on and anything between 10 and 20 days. Would you be available to come back for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm a dentist. I have my own practice. This was a waste of time for me, and I've come to help as much as I could. This is an enormous effort for me because of my ill health. I only work three hours a day when I'm at home. And over the past three days, I have been working almost 24 hours a day. Under such conditions, I would not be able to come back again. I'm here. And if there's anything I can do now, I'll do my best to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, if I would tell you that most likely if you would come back, you would arrive, let's say, one day, be examined the next morning, and perhaps even be able to travel back, of course we have to look at the schedules, whether that's possible. But it would not be a similar couple of days that would be needed. The examination -- there would be no further preparation for that. Just you would be required to answer questions in Court and no preparation for that, and just going back. Would that be possible for you? So presumably, it might be able to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I can't walk. I am an ill man. This has been a huge effort for me. And in addition to that, I've had to close my house, my son is on his own. But he can't do anything without me. We have a huge laboratory. We have a practice that I am in charge of. This has been a huge sacrifice for me, coming here to help you. Unfortunately, I won't be able to do it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, this, Mr. Harmon, creates a new situation which perhaps we could better discuss in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There are, of course, alternatives. Videolink is a possibility. I don't know other possibilities other than that. I would suggest that that be considered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, of course, it's -- if the witness would not be available. And I'm just inquiring, one of the things that has been done now and then in this Tribunal is that people would testify in a studio with a videolink, so that would take you then, I would say exactly the same time. Perhaps you would have to travel to Banja Luka, but a short distance, and then to be examined by a videolink between The Hague and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Would that be something that would be possible for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Banja Luka is certainly closer. And I would consider going to Banja Luka if I'm informed exactly when I'm supposed to be there. If there's a slot given to me in advance, then yes, I would be able to travel there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there anything at this moment that should be discussed in the presence of the witness? Apart from that, I'll instruct him -- yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Given what Mr. Biscevic says about his personal life, his personal health, and his dental practice, it would be perhaps of assistance to Mr. Biscevic if we could identify at least the dates now when the Court would consider a videolink possibility in Banja Luka, so he can make the appropriate schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I do think the witness should be asked to leave straight away now. We've already had enough discussion in front of the witness. Appreciate that his own personal convenience comes into it, but I suggest it's no longer appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I think that at this moment, to go into those details would not be something that could not be done if at all needed at a later stage and through other means. I'll instruct the witness on what to do. Mr. Biscevic, as you well have understood, the parties and the Chamber will have to consider further how to proceed in respect of cross-examination of you. You are at this moment, therefore, perhaps in the middle of your testimony. You have been examined by counsel for the Prosecution, not yet examined by counsel for the Defence. I'd like to instruct you that at this stage, and you should not speak with anyone about the testimony you have given, also not about the testimony that still would come. So refrain from speaking to anyone about the testimony. You'll be informed through the witness and victims section, and you might even be consulted about certain matters, as soon as possible so that it will be clear to you as well how this Chamber would like to proceed. And I noticed that you said that you're not available to come back to The Hague, partly due to your health and to your personal circumstances, and that you would consider to be examined by -- through a videolink from the area. For the time being, therefore, I thank you for having come to The Hague, especially since you explained to us that it was not easy, both in view of health and your professional duties, and it might also not have been easy for you in respect of your family situation on which you testified until now. The Chamber will not speak about that at this moment since you're in the middle. But certainly there's understanding that this is not just easy. So you're excused. You'll hear from the Tribunal soon about whether and how we would proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please escort Mr. Biscevic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness now has left the courtroom. Before we address the other matters that were still on our agenda, I would like to give an opportunity to the parties - and to the extent they can do in open session, fine, if they think we should turn into private session, I'll hear from them - on the issue of how we should proceed with the testimony of Mr. Biscevic. I think, Mr. Harmon, you at least gave a suggestion for an alternative, and I felt that the Defence would like to say something more about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I only reiterate, Your Honour, that the sooner Mr. Biscevic is informed of the dates, the sooner he can make plans to accommodate his personal situation. And that's my only request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One of the practical reasons why I refrained from giving any follow-up to your suggestion is that setting up a videolink requires quite a lot of matters, like someone being present there, availability of technical facilities, et cetera. So therefore, for that reason already, I thought that it was not of that much use to continue that immediately. But I can imagine, Mr. Stewart, that you have different views on how to proceed. Could you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, yes, in this sense, that with respect, Your Honour, we suggest that the witness's quite natural irritation I think he displayed, but we all do that sometimes, about the fact that he'd have to come back doesn't mean that what he says shouldn't perhaps be treated with a little bit of skepticism as far as his health is concerned, perhaps. He came here once, and he can come here another time. I don't wish to be harsh about it. But inconvenience to witnesses is inevitably a feature of these serious trials. And to simply accept on his say-so that he has a health problem preventing comeback, it's just, well, the evidence is that he doesn't because he was here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the mere fact that he's here doesn't say that he doesn't have a health problem, but at least not such a health problem that didn't prevent him from coming once.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's exactly what I meant. I don't mean that his health may be perfect, I simply have no idea. But clearly, it doesn't prevent him from being here. I 100 per cent agree with Mr. Harmon. Of course, in fairness to the witness and everybody, the more notice he's given of the more specific date -- and we will cooperate so far as our cooperation is needed, as fully as possible - but that goes for every single witness anyway - but so far as videolink is concerned, we don't necessarily have strong views on that. We apprehend that there is a preference on significant evidence to have a live witness in court. Although, it no longer requires him to be here to be interviewed by the Prosecution might cause less trouble if they didn't come here for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the Defence prefers the witness to be recalled and appear in The Hague and not to be examined -- cross-examined by videolink. And Mr. Harmon, I take it that you only made the suggestion for an alternative on the assumption that the primary aim of getting the witness back in The Hague would fail. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have this discussion in private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't follow that at all. It's difficult to see why there's any reason to have this discussion in private session. We're not going into any health details --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, let's hear the reasons for the private session in private session because --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can't resist that, having expressed an initial reaction, I'll reserve my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When we were in private session, counsel for the Prosecution explained what he knew about the health situation of the witness, and then counsel for the Defence opposed against dealing with Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond this matter in private session and asked for a ruling and the Chamber will give that ruling, main objection being that there was no detail whatsoever, nothing that could not have been dealt with in open session. Upon further explanation by the OTP, the Chamber established that at least part of what had been said was already a part of the testimony of the witness. The Chamber will give a ruling on whether or not it is necessary to make that part of the transcript public. Apart from that, is there -- I think the Chamber will consider at this moment whether -- how to proceed. And that means that the Chamber will consider whether it would seek further information, perhaps through the Victims and Witness Unit on whether it should allow the witness to complete his testimony through videolink where the Defence seems to have a clear preference for -- clear preference for further viva voce cross-examination, where the Prosecution would think that there are good reasons to accept the statement of the witness that for the reasons he mentioned he's not available for cross-examination in The Hague. We'll consider the matter, and we'll let you know. We'll let the parties know. Then, having dealt with that issue, Mr. Tieger, I'd like to turn into private session again for the other issues still pending.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we go into private session, may I just ask something. First of all, Your Honour said the Chamber will give a ruling on whether it's necessary to make that part of the transcript public. In other words, the part that coincides with evidence that has already been given. Do I understand that the Trial Chamber is therefore ruling that the other part of what was said in private session just now should remain in private session? Or is that still open?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's still open. I would say it was mainly to say that the part we dealt with in private session, whether that should remain private, or whether it could be made public without any further specification on the specific parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that. May I again comment, again I'm trying to be as careful as I can in this area, notwithstanding my submission. I recognise that at the moment as things stand a certain amount of things have been said in private session. But the witness after all himself in open session referred to the reasons for his not wishing to come back and give evidence and referred to his health. Just this, Your Honour, that it is absolutely standard practice, we suggest, that there must be a medical certificate in relation to such matters, that a witness's say-so that for some reason he really can't come back, although he has already been here once, if there is a compelling reason, and that is what's being suggested in this case for the matter to be dealt with by videolink rather than by live evidence, stronger support of the reasons is needed. And we would simply, because in the middle of what I was saying, then Your Honour invited Mr. Harmon to comment, what the witness says about his working life, according to him the most that he's going to lose in terms of work is three hours, because that's what he says he does a day. Well, maybe six hours if it's not possible to do it quite as quickly as Your Honour indicated, though it does seem, on the basis of where we are, that the likelihood of this witness being able to travel one afternoon - no doubt, there's three hours in the morning - and go back pretty quick is quite high. Whether it's three hours or six hours, my point is only this, Your Honour, that hours of work lost by witnesses at that level are simply standard. It's inconvenient. It's a nuisance. Nobody wants it. But then Mr. Krajisnik is facing something rather different from that if he is ever convicted. So Your Honour, it's standard. Witnesses, we're afraid, have to accept inconvenience. That goes with the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you gave further reasons to explain why I already established that the preference of the Defence was that the witness would reappear viva voce. Then we'll turn to the other matters, and we'll have to turn to private session. And I am looking to the booth whether we could still go on for -- I hope not more than ten minutes. This will prevent us from coming back this afternoon. If there's any problem, then I'd like to hear about it. We now turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 20th day of September, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.53 p.m.,
